For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta Method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the slope at $$
\displaystyle ({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),
$$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the slope at $$
\displaystyle ({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),
$$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of 

$$
Δx=1-0=1.
$$

First, we create a table and add the initial condition data.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now let's find the required values.

- First, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3x(y-2) \\  & =3(0)(1-2) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ |  |  |  |  |

- The first intermediate point is

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1},{y}_{1}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1,\,1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0\cdot 1) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2},1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first intermediate slope is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′} & =3{x}_{1}({y}_{1}-2) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (1-2) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  |  |

- The second intermediate point is

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{2},{y}_{2}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1,\,1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \,\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)\cdot 1) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second intermediate slope is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & =3{x}_{2}({y}_{2}-2) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}-2) \\  & =-\frac{21}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-\frac{3}{2}$ | $-\frac{21}{8}$ |  |  |

- The third intermediate point is

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+1,\,1+\left(-\frac{21}{8}\right)\cdot 1) \\  & =(1,-\frac{13}{8}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third intermediate slope is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{3}^{′} & =3{x}_{3}({y}_{3}-2) \\  & =3(1)(-\frac{13}{8}-2) \\  & =-\frac{87}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-\frac{3}{2}$ | $-\frac{21}{8}$ | $-\frac{87}{8}$ |  |

- Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the Runge-Kutta Method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(0+2\cdot \,\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)+2\cdot \,\left(-\frac{21}{8}\right)+\left(-\frac{87}{8}\right))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\,-\frac{24}{8}-\frac{42}{8}-\frac{87}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \,\left(-\frac{153}{8}\right) \\  & =-\frac{51}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-\frac{3}{2}$ | $-\frac{21}{8}$ | $-\frac{87}{8}$ | $-\frac{51}{16}$ |

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =1+\left(-\frac{51}{16}\right) \\  & =-\frac{35}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these rows to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-\frac{3}{2}$ | $-\frac{21}{8}$ | $-\frac{87}{8}$ | $-\frac{51}{16}$ |
| $1$ | $-\frac{35}{16}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈-\frac{35}{16}.$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Notice that its augmented matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\  & =2(\frac{3}{2}{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3} \\  & =6{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}6{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=2,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{2}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}+2x+1}{{x}^{2}-x-12} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(x+\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(1-\frac{1}{x}-\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{2}{x},\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\frac{1}{x}$ and $\frac{12}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(x+\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(1-\frac{1}{x}-\frac{12}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ≈\frac{x+0+0}{1-0-0} \\  & =\frac{x}{1} \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

As $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{3}$ then $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }=\frac{3}{5}.$

Let's sketch our angle $\theta $ in the coordinate plane.

![](images/aa/aaba5af0542d29ef91d4b0e17907a81e32bccc402c48b32c205e7298630b5bc0.png)

We're given that $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{5}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$ we have:

- $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}=-\frac{4}{3}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}{\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

Finally, we have

$\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{3}-\frac{3}{4}=-\frac{25}{12}.$

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+2x-3}{{x}^{3}-x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{1}{x},\frac{2}{{x}^{2}},\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0-0}{1-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

The intermediate value theorem can be applied on closed intervals on which the function is continuous. 

The function $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ is discontinuous at the values of $x$ which make the denominator $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ equal to zero. Therefore, $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi $, where $n$ is any integer.

- On the interval $[0,1],$ we **can** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

- On the interval $[1,2],$ we **cannot** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ because this interval contains the point of discontinuity $\frac{\pi }{2}≈1.57\,.$

- On the interval $[-1,0),$ we **cannot** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ because this interval is not closed.

Therefore, the correct answer is $[0,1]$ only.

The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A) &={R}^{n} \\ \text{dim(Col}(A)) &=n=\text{rank}(A) \\ \text{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) &=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has no inverse.* $\,✓$  

Indeed,  a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{rank}(A)=n.$*$\,\times$

Since our matrix is not invertible, according to the invertible matrix theorem, it must be $\text{rank}(A)\ne n.$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.*  $\,\times$

Since $\text{rank}(A)\ne n$, it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))<n,$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$A$ has no inverse” only.

Let's look at each statement in turn.

- The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with simple harmonic motion (SHM) under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky.
$$

Rearranging the above equation gives

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{k}{m}y=0.
$$

Comparing this to the SHM equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0,
$$

we see that

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{k}{m}.
$$

Substituting our values for $k$ and $m$ gives

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{8}{32}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\omega =\frac{1}{2}
$$

So the governing differential equation is

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{4}y=0.
$$

Hence, statement “The governing differential equation is ${y}^{″}+\frac{1}{4}y=0$” is true.

- The frequency $f$ (measured in ${s}^{-1}$) is given by

$$
f=\frac{1}{T}=\frac{\omega }{2\pi },
$$

where $T$ is the period. So in our case, we have

$$
f=\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2\pi }=\frac{1}{4\pi }\,.
$$

So the frequency $f=\frac{1}{4\pi }\,{\text{s}}^{-1}.$
Hence, statement “The frequency $f$ of the oscillation is $f=\frac{1}{4\pi }\,{\text{s}}^{-1}$” is true.

- The general solution for $y(t)$ can take one of three forms.

- $A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

- $R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+{ϕ}_{1})$

- $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+{ϕ}_{2})$

Writing $\omega =\frac{1}{2}$ in form 1 gives

$$
y(t)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{t}{2}+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{t}{2}.
$$

Hence, statement “The general solution can be expressed as $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{t}{4}+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{t}{4}$ where $R$ is the amplitude and $ϕ$ is the phase” is false.

So, the correct answer is “The governing differential equation is ${y}^{″}+\frac{1}{4}y=0$”; “The frequency $f$ of the oscillation is $f=\frac{1}{4\pi }\,{\text{s}}^{-1}$” only.

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{2}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. Therefore $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

Using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we finally get

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}=1.
$$

Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}.$ If $k\ne 1$, then

$$
det(A)=det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}=1-k\ne 0.
$$

So, according to the invertible matrix theorem $A$ is invertible and $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ is the unique solution of  $Ax=0.$
Also, the system 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
has exactly one solution, and the lines $x+y=0$ and $x+ky=0$ intersect at exactly one point.

*If $k\ne 1$, then the system $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ has the unique zero solution.* $\,✓$

before:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2x-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2y+6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x-2,\,2y+6,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-2 &=0 \\ 2y+6 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=1$ while the second equation gives $y=-3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into our function, we get

$$
z={1}^{2}-2(1)+(-3)^{2}+6(-3)+10=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(1,-3,0).$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho $, $\theta $, and $ϕ$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{z}{\rho }
$$

First, we find $\rho :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(x,y)=(1,-\sqrt{3})$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So to find $\theta ,$ we first need to find the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{1}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi $ to get $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $ϕ$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{z}{\rho }\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $U$ are $(2\sqrt{2},\frac{5\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{4}).$

For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j+z(t)k$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({t}^{2}-2t)p(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t)\cdot p(t)+({t}^{2}-2t)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p(t)) \\  & =(2t-2)\,p(t)+({t}^{2}-2t)\,{p}^{′}(t) \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =(2(1)-2)\,p(1)+((1)^{2}-2(1))\,{p}^{′}(1) \\  & =0-{p}^{′}(1) \\  & =-(2\,i-\,j-2\,k) \\  & =-2i+\,j+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(1):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}‖r(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(1):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(1)}{‖{r}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-2\,i+j+2k) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector to the curve at the point that corresponds to $t=1$ is  $T(1)=-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k.$

$$

before:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,k,$ then along the curve we have $x=t,$ $y=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},$ and $z=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)\,k \\  & =i+t\,j+t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{y+z}{x}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}}{t}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+2{t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=4t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{3}^{5}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({5}^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{5}-3\sqrt{3}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

before: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
after:
Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $$
\displaystyle \frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

before:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A) &={R}^{n} \\ \text{dim(Col}(A)) &=n=\text{rank}(A) \\ \text{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) &=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $A$ is **not** invertible.* $\,\times$

By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ we must have that $A$ is invertible.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{rank}(A)=n.$* $\,✓$ 

Indeed, since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{rank}(A)=\text{dim(Col}(A))=n.$

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}.$* $\,✓$

Indeed, since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{rank}(A)=n$; $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}$ only.

A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Let's attempt to write $\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y}$ in the standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\left(\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2y+{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is in standard form with  $P(x)=-2$ and $Q(x)={x}^{2}.$ Since the equation is written in standard form, we conclude that it is a first-order linear ODE.

All of the other equations cannot be written in the standard form, and therefore they are not first-order linear ODEs.

Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution.  Let $u={x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{-u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each integral in turn.

- Statement “${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent” is true. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }({-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}|}_{0}^{a}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-{e}^{-{a}^{2}}+{e}^{0}) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the integral converges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is false. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(-{e}^{0}+{e}^{-{a}^{2}}) \\  & =-1+0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the integral converges.

- Statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” is false. The integral in statement “${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent” can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1-1=0.
$$

So the integral converges.

In conclusion, only statement “${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent” is true.

$$
x(6)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t=9.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(6)=-2+9=7
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=6$ is $x=7.$

First, let's start by defining a new variable $X$ as

$$
X=4x+\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

So, we need to calculate $X$-values at the maxima of

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡X.
$$

 

The $X$-values at the maxima are given by the following expression:

$$
X=\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi 
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the $x$-values at the maxima of our original function, we rewrite $X$ in terms of the original variable $x$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi  \\ 4x+\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi  \\ 4x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{16}+n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the values of $x$ that maximize $f(x)$ are given by $x=\frac{\pi }{16}+n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2},$ where $n$ is an integer.

before:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ g(y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C.
$$

$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
3{x}^{2}+4x-7=0\,\text{and}\,{6}^{x-2}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $3{x}^{2}+4x-7=0$ can be factored as

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$

A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is NOT the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}.$

We see that it is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2.$

Hence, the original differential equation is  NOT homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,
$$

We can check that this is not homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)\ne f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}}{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}f(x,y)\,\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)\ne f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is NOT homogeneous.

Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “$F$ is closed under matrix addition” is true. If ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ are two matrices from $F,$ then ${A}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}{A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}{A}_{2}.$ So, we have 

$$

Let's apply the general algorithm to find the power series solution for the following equation:

$$
y' - y  =0
$$

- **Step 1:** First, we write the solution as a general power series $y =\displaystyle{\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n}.$

- **Step 2:** Next, we compute $y'$ so that we can substitute the general series solution into the differential equation. Computing $y',$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & ={({\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n})}^{′} \\  & ={({a}_{0}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n})}^{′} \\  & =0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}{x}^{n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}{x}^{n-1},\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting in the differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}-y & =0 \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}{x}^{n-1}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 3:** Then, we rewrite all the series in the equation so that they use the same index of summation, the powers of $x$ are the same, and the indices start at the same value. In the first sum, we change the index of the summation by writing $m = n-1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{m=0}^{\infty }(m+1){a}_{m+1}{x}^{m}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $m$ with $n$ in the first summation (since it does not matter which letter we use) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(n+1){a}_{n+1}{x}^{n}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 4:** We consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$ Since both sums now start with $n=0,$ we can combine them as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(n+1){a}_{n+1}{x}^{n}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} & =0 \\ {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }[(n+1){a}_{n+1}{x}^{n}-{a}_{n}{x}^{n}] & =0 \\ {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }[(n+1){a}_{n+1}-{a}_{n}]{x}^{n} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(n+1){a}_{n+1}-{a}_{n} & =0 \\ {a}_{n+1} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{n+1},\,n=0,1,2…\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(n+1){a}_{n+1}{x}^{n}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n} & =0 \\ {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }[(n+1){a}_{n+1}{x}^{n}-{a}_{n}{x}^{n}] & =0 \\ {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }[(n+1){a}_{n+1}-{a}_{n}]{x}^{n} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 5:** Setting the coefficients of the series equal to $0,$ we get the following recurrence relation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(n+1){a}_{n+1}-{a}_{n} & =0 \\ {a}_{n+1} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{n+1},\,n=0,1,2…\end{aligned}
$$

In the following, we'll see how to apply this recurrence relation to find the final power series solution of the differential equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (2x+1)\cdot {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =(2x+1)\cdot \frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}-\int \frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

Substituting $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨6,5⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$

$$

$$

For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{0}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is true. Since statements “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” and ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$”; ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$; “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function”.

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\left\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}\right.$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “If $\text{rank}(T)=2,$ then $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$” is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{n}$ into ${R}^{n},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\left\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=n \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}\right.$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “If $\text{Ker}(T)={⟨x,y,z⟩\,|\,x+y=0}$ then $\text{rank}(T)+1=n$” is false. Solving $x+y=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=-y.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-y \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=y\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{v}_{1}}+z\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ \text{rank}(T)+2 & =n.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “If there exists a vector $v\notin \text{Im}(T),$ then $|T|\ne 0$” is false. If $v\notin \text{Im}(T)$ then $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{n}$, so, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $T$ is not a bijection. Thus, the matrix $T$ is not invertible, and, consequently, $|T|=0.$

$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

All four sample slopes are already computed. So, we just need to find the increment on $y.$

We compute $Δy$ using the Runge-Kutta method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(1+2\cdot \frac{9}{4}+2\cdot \frac{51}{16}+\frac{67}{8})\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{81}{4} \\  & =\frac{27}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{9}{4}$ | $\frac{51}{16}$ | $\frac{67}{8}$ | $\frac{27}{8}$ |

$$

$$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{9}{4}$ | $\frac{51}{16}$ | $\frac{67}{8}$ | $\frac{27}{8}$ |
| $1$ | $\frac{35}{8}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1)≈\frac{35}{8}.\end{aligned}

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{x} & \frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{y}{x})=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(e,e),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(e,e)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{e} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{e}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $D$ the diameter of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the diameter $D$ of the circle. Since $D=2r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $D$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {\left(\frac{D}{2}\right)}^{2}=\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}D}\left(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2} \\ \frac{2}{5} & =\frac{\pi D}{2} \\ D & =\frac{4}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $D=2r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2r & =\frac{4}{5\pi } \\ r & =\frac{2}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

- If the sum of the outcomes is $6$ ($(1,5),(2,4),(3,3),(4,2)$, or $(5,1)$), the player wins $$6,$ so we have $p=6.$

- If the sum of the outcomes is not $6,$ the player loses $$1,$ so we have $p=-1.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

before: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$  that satisfies $y(1)=1.$

We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =-(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)+C} \\ 1 & =-\frac{1}{\frac{\pi }{4}+C} \\ C & =-\frac{\pi }{4}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)-\frac{\pi }{4}-1}=\frac{4}{\pi +4-4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}.
$$

$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero.

$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)=-2+2=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/21/212435c94989d0553db86b8d39edae3a7905d41ef668bb33fa0a62bed99d5462.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(-1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-2x=1-2(-1)=3, \\ Q(x,y) & =2y=2(2t-1)=4t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)=0, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3)\cdot (2)-(4t-2)\cdot (0)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot {[t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\cdot (1-0) \\  & =6\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=6.
$$

$$

$$

$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $7\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{1}^{2}]-[{0}^{2}] \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is true. Since statements “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$” and ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=6I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=1\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=6I+\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+6I=10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+6{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))+6(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-3\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+(6\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +6\beta &=10\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ 6\alpha +3\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{2}{3},$ $\beta =\frac{4}{3}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-6t}-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)}^{2}}≈1.49\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

The Chinese remainder theorem states that if the natural numbers ${n}_{1},{n}_{2},…,{n}_{k}$ are pairwise coprime, meaning that $\text{gcd}({n}_{i},{n}_{j})=1$ whenever $i\ne j,$ then for any integers ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},…,{a}_{k}$ the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡{a}_{1} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{1}) \\ x≡{a}_{2} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{2}) \\ \,⋮ \\ x≡{a}_{k} & (\text{mod}\,{n}_{k})\end{aligned}\right.
$$

has a unique solution modulo ${n}_{1}{n}_{2}⋯{n}_{k}.$

Let's now inspect each of the given systems in turn.

- The theorem does *not* apply to system $\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡4 & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x≡5 & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}\right.$ since $6$ and $8$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(6,8)=2>1
$$

- The theorem applies to system $\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡14 & (\text{mod}\,16)\end{aligned}\right.$. The numbers $3,$ and $16$ are pairwise coprime natural numbers. Therefore, according to the Chinese remainder theorem, the system has a unique solution modulo $3\cdot 16=48.$

- The theorem does *not* apply to system $\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡3 & (\text{mod}\,4) \\ x≡7 & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}\right.$ since $4$ and $12$ are not coprime: 

$$
\text{gcd}(4,12)=4>1
$$

So, the correct answer is $\left\{\begin{aligned}x≡2 & (\text{mod}\,3) \\ x≡14 & (\text{mod}\,16)\end{aligned}\right.$ only

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{5}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{5},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3}{8{x}^{5}+x-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{5}})}{(\frac{8{x}^{5}}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{x}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{5}})}{(8+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{2}{{x}^{3}},\frac{3}{{x}^{5}},\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{5}})}{(8+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{8+0-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{r}_{22}}{{q}_{12}}=\frac{\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\right)}{\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\right)}=2.$

For an initial value problem

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=f(x,y,z),\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=g(x,y,z),\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Euler's method approximates the solution by applying the update rule component-wise to each equation. More precisely, the increments on $y$ and $z$ are

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}Δy &={y}^{′}\cdot Δx, \\ Δz &={z}^{′}\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The new values are then given by ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}=z+Δz.$

First, because the initial conditions are $y(0)=1$ and $z(0)=-1,$ we place $y=1$ and $z=-1$ in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  | $-1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x+y+3z \\  & =2\cdot 0+1+3\cdot (-1) \\  & =0+1-3 \\  & =-2 \\ {z}^{′} & =x-y+2z \\  & =0-1+2\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1-2 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ |  | $-1$ | $-3$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-3)\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-1$ | $-3$ | $-\frac{3}{4}$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=1+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-1+\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)=-\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-1$ | $-3$ | $-\frac{3}{4}$ |
| $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  | $-\frac{7}{4}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y\,\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)≈\frac{1}{2}$
and
$z\,\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)≈-\frac{7}{4}.$

The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}
$$

is the first Frobenius solution, and the second Frobenius solution is determined as follows:

- **Case 1**: If ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}\notin Z,$ then 
${y}_{2}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{2}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{2}){x}^{n}.$

- **Case 2**: If ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2},$ then
${y}_{2}(x)={y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n}.$

- **Case 3**: If ${\lambda }_{1}-{\lambda }_{2}\in N,$ then
${y}_{2}(x)={b}_{-1}{y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{{\lambda }_{2}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $4{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +3=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +3 & =0 \\ (2\lambda -1)(2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={b}_{-1}{y}_{1}(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{1/2}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}{x}^{n},
$$

where the constants ${b}_{n}$ are found by substitution.

If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then the method of Frobenius states that there is at least one solution of the form

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n},
$$

where $\lambda $ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants.

Substituting this solution and its derivatives into the ODE, collecting like terms, and setting coefficients equal to zero, we obtain: 

- the indicial equation from the coefficients of the $n=0$ term for arbitrary ${a}_{0},$ and

- a recurrence formula from the coefficients of the $n\ge 1$ terms.

**Step 1**: Write the solution $y$ as a Frobenius power series:

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}$ and ${y}^{″}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={({\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n})}^{′}={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1} \\ {y}^{″} & ={({\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1})}^{′}={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n-1)(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Rewrite all the series in the equation so that they use the same index of summation, the powers of $x$ are the same, and the indices start at the same value.

The terms of the differential equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}6x{y}^{″} & =6x\cdot {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n-1)(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-2} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }6((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}, \\ 5{y}^{′} & =5\cdot {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }5(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}, \\ -y & =-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the $y$ term, we change the index of the summation by writing $n=m-1.$ This gives

$$
-y=-{\sum }_{m=1}^{\infty }{a}_{m-1}{x}^{\lambda +m-1}.
$$

Then, replacing $m$ with $n$ (since it does not matter which letter we use) gives

$$
-y=-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n-1}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}.
$$

Now, isolating the $n=0$ terms for the other terms in the ODE, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6x{y}^{″} & =6({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }6((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}, \\ 5{y}^{′} & =5\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda -1}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }5(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $2$nd and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}({3}^{2+1}-9)=\frac{1}{2}(18)=9.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 2.$

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $4\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=4\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=4I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=4I+4q+\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(4I+4q+\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I=39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+4{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+4(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ +4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ (-5\alpha +12\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-12\alpha -5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha +12\beta &=39\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -12\alpha -5\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{15}{13}$ and $\beta =\frac{36}{13}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t}-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{15}{13}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{36}{13}\right)}^{2}}=3.
$$

The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$

$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨3,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,3)-f(0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨3,3⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\ \sqrt{25-{3}^{2}}-\sqrt{25-{0}^{2}} & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,3⟩ \\ 4-5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,3⟩ \\ -1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-\frac{x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}},0⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-\frac{{c}_{1}}{\sqrt{25-{c}_{1}^{2}}},0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Substituting $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨1,1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1)-f(0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\ 6-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1⟩ \\ 6 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨24{x}^{3}{y}^{3},\,18{x}^{4}{y}^{2}⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨24{{c}_{1}}^{3}{{c}_{2}}^{3},\,18{{c}_{1}}^{4}{{c}_{2}}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}

Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$

$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

$$

$$

We need to find the maximum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=2x+3y+2z
$$

subject to the constraints  

$$
g(x,y,z)=2x-y-z=-1,\,h(x,y,z)={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=-1 \\ h(x,y,z) &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨2,3,2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2,-1,-1⟩+\mu ⟨0,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2 &=2\lambda \\ 3 &=-\lambda +2\mu y \\ 2 &=-\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\lambda &=1 \\ y &=\frac{2}{\mu } \\ z &=\frac{3}{2\mu }\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction.

Next, we substitute our expressions for $y$ and $z$ into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{4}{{\mu }^{2}}+\frac{9}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{25}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ {\mu }^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \mu  & =\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=\pm \frac{4}{5},\,z=\pm \frac{3}{5}.
$$

- If $y=\frac{4}{5}$ and $z=\frac{3}{5},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y-z & =-1 \\ 2x-\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5} & =-1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{5}. \\  & \end{aligned}
$$

- If $y=-\frac{4}{5}$ and $z=-\frac{3}{5},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y-z & =-1 \\ 2x-\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)-\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right) & =-1 \\ 2x & =-\frac{12}{5} \\ x & =-\frac{6}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$

| --- | --- | --- |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(\frac{1}{5},\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}),$ and its maximum value is $4.$

$$

$$

Proving that the base case is true is usually straightforward. We simply calculate the left-hand and right-hand sides independently and show they're equal.

Next, we write down our **inductive hypothesis**. We assume that $P(k)$ is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$ To do this, we simply replace $n$ with $k$ in our original statement $P(n).$

Recall the following classifications of recurrence relations:

- The order of a relation ${a}_{n}$ is the largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms in the relation.

- A recurrence relation is *linear (with constant coefficients)* if it expresses ${a}_{n}$ as a sum of previous terms ${a}_{n-1},…,{a}_{n-k}$ with constant coefficients, together with possibly a final term that depends only on $n:$

$$
{a}_{n}={s}_{1}{a}_{n-1}+{s}_{2}{a}_{n-2}+…+{s}_{k}{a}_{n-k}+g(n)
$$

where ${s}_{1},{s}_{2},…,{s}_{k}$ are constants and $g(n)$ is a function, often called a *forcing function*, that does not involve ${a}_{n}$ or its preceding terms.

- A linear recurrence relation (with constant coefficients) is *homogeneous* if the forcing function is zero. Otherwise, it is *inhomogeneous.*

Let's classify the relation ${a}_{n}=\frac{{a}_{n-1}}{2}+\frac{{a}_{n-2}}{3}-4.$

- The largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms ${a}_{n-1}$ and ${a}_{n-2}$ in the relation is $2.$ So, the relation has order $2.$

- The previous terms ${a}_{n-1}$ and ${a}_{n-2}$ occur only in the first power and their  coefficients are constants. So, the relation is linear.

- The relation is linear, and the forcing function $g(n)=-4$ is nonzero. So, the relation is inhomogeneous.

Therefore, the recurrence relation ${a}_{n}$ has order
$2,$
is
$\text{linear},$
and is
$\text{inhomogeneous}.$

$$

$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$

$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-20\lambda m+100{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-10\lambda )(m-10\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=10\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{10\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{10\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{10\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda x}+B{e}^{10\lambda x}+10B\lambda x{e}^{10\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda } & =0 \\ 10A\lambda +B+10B\lambda  & =0 \\ (10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{20\lambda }+2B{e}^{20\lambda }+2(10A\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }+B{e}^{20\lambda }+20B\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(10A\lambda +B+20B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+20A\lambda +2B+40B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+(4+40\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}10\lambda  & 1+10\lambda  \\ 1+20\lambda  & 4(1+10\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}10\lambda \cdot 4(1+10\lambda )-(1+10\lambda )(1+20\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -(1+20\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -1-20\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )(20\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$

$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+5| & <1 \\ -1<x+5 & <1 \\ -6<x & <-4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the radius of convergence is $R=1,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-6,-4).$

$$

$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-4+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{1}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+n}\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the above series with  $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}},
$$
we see that the series is convergent by the comparison test.

So the interval of convergence is $I=[-6,-4].$
